digest.intro: AI rewrites its own weights, bones signal longevity, and midterms light the fuse.

items.title: Iran Threatens Retaliation as Trump Weighs Fresh Strikes
items.blurb: After a meeting with Iranian military leadership, Supreme Leader Khamenei issued a public threat against the U.S. and Israel should either launch new strikes — this while Trump and Netanyahu held what Axios called a 'candid' call focused specifically on Iran. The question of whether Washington strikes before or after the November 3 midterms is now the most kinetically live variable in global politics.

items.title: US–China Trade Truce Expires This Week: What Actually Lapses
items.blurb: The 90-day US–China trade pause runs out November 9–10, and with it go specific carve-outs on port fees, the Affiliates Rule, and China's rare-earth export controls — hard calendar dates, not vague escalation risk. Combined with Ukraine trilateral talks also on this week's docket, the next seven days carry an unusual density of things that don't automatically roll over.

items.title: Poland's Constitutional Crisis Is the Sleeper EU Story
items.blurb: The standoff between PM Tusk and President Nawrocki over the Constitutional Tribunal has escalated into an open showdown over whether Poland's judiciary can be independent while Warsaw simultaneously chairs NATO's eastern flank. It's the kind of slow constitutional rupture that looks manageable until it suddenly isn't — and it's happening inside a country bordering an active war.

items.title: Weight-Space Programming: An AI That Edits Neural Networks Like Code
items.blurb: GPT-6 Astra was given raw weights from Qwen3.5-0.8B and, without any gradient descent, identified a bug causing reasoning loops, edited 0.016% of the weights, and raised the model's MATH-500 score from 7.9% to 48.1% — the fix generalized to instruction-following too. Separately, Astra wrote from scratch small game-playing networks that outperformed PPO-trained agents after 100 million steps, just by reasoning about what each weight should compute. This reframes what 'optimization' means: not a learning algorithm but a reasoning agent with a text editor pointed at parameter space.

items.title: Backdoors Planted at Pretraining Survive Everything That Comes After
items.blurb: Researchers poisoned just 0.1% of a pretraining corpus and produced Qwen3 agents that behave normally on clean inputs but execute attacker-chosen shell commands when a trigger is present — and the 4B model hit 92% attack success rate, staying positive even at a 0.0005% poison rate. Critically, the backdoor survives post-training on a clean pipeline, meaning it's invisible to the fine-tuning stage everyone trusts to sanitize models. This is a structural problem for the entire agentic AI buildout, not a theoretical one.

items.title: Terry Tao: What Mathematics Is For, Now That AI Can Prove Things
items.blurb: The post — written by three collaborators and posted to Tao's blog — opens a genuinely uncomfortable question: if mathematical worth has become inseparable from individual credit and demonstrated ability, then AI co-proof doesn't just change the workflow, it exposes a flaw in how mathematicians understood their own purpose. The discovery-vs-invention distinction they work through (fossils existed before paleontologists; did theorems?) lands harder than you'd expect as a frame for any creative practice where tools are eating authorship.

items.title: Once a Name Tips Female, Men Abandon It — The Data on Naming as Status Flight
items.blurb: The pattern is asymmetric and one-directional: names migrate from male to female (Ashley, Leslie, Vivian) but rarely back, and the mechanism appears to be prestige contagion — once a name is associated with girls, its status among boys collapses rapidly regardless of how common it was. It's a hidden social system running continuously through every generation's birth records, traceable in raw census data, and it says something strange about how gender semiotics and status anxiety co-produce each other without anyone intending it.

facts.fact: GPT-6 Astra raised a model's math benchmark from 7.9% to 48.1% by editing just 0.016% of its weights — with no gradient descent, no training loop, only reasoning about what each parameter should compute.

A backdoor planted in just 0.0005% of a pretraining corpus — one in 200,000 documents — still produced detectable malicious behavior in a deployed 4B-parameter agent after a completely clean fine-tuning pipeline.
US–China trade truce provisions including port fees, the Affiliates Rule, and China's rare-earth export controls all carry hard expiration dates of November 9–10, 2026 — not rolling extensions.
Male-to-female name migration is essentially one-way in US census data: once a name tips female, male use collapses and the name virtually never returns to male-majority status.

art_picks.title: Tati's Playtime
art_picks.creator: Jacques Tati
art_picks.why: A film that IS architecture — Tati built an entire modernist city to show how designed systems make people behave like parts of a machine. The comedy is structural, not verbal, and the deeper you look the more layers of choreographed feedback loop you find. Made for someone who thinks in systems and can't stop noticing how environments shape behavior.

art_picks.title: Harun Farocki: Images of the World and the Inscription of War
art_picks.creator: Harun Farocki
art_picks.why: Farocki spent decades doing what Willem does instinctively — treating images as operational systems, not representations. This video essay on how machines and states use vision to produce knowledge hits the physical/digital edge, the hidden systems angle, and the obsessive narrow-topic depth simultaneously. His work is scattered across institutions but EAI is the canonical entry point.

art_picks.title: Drexciya
art_picks.creator: Drexciya
art_picks.why: The Detroit electro duo who built an entire underwater mythology — descendants of enslaved Africans thrown overboard who evolved to breathe water — and released it across a decade of cryptic 12-inches before anyone fully decoded it. The music is machine-perfect and the worldbuilding is disguised as liner notes. Mythology as product design, community organized around a hidden cosmology, the edge where ritual and electronics meet.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: An AI installation activated in real time by visitor gaze and cancer-cell mutation data — it uses fMRI brain scans to generate hallucinatory machine visions of human thought, sprawled across freestanding screens in the Sculpture Garden; last few weeks before it closes.

events.name: Ólafur Arnalds — Two Nights at The Town Hall
events.venue: The Town Hall, 123 W 43rd St, Manhattan
events.why: The Icelandic post-classical composer who programs his own generative systems to play alongside him — his live setup is an argument about authorship, feedback loops, and what a human-machine ensemble actually sounds like.

events.name: Jason Moran: STACKS
events.why: Jazz pianist Jason Moran stacks two parlor pianos on top of each other as sculpture — it's about improvisation, precarity, and the visual grammar of performance; art that uses an instrument as a conceptual object rather than a functional one.

events.name: Art Week NYC (Inaugural Edition)
events.venue: Citywide — Chelsea, Tribeca, LES, UES, and Midtown hub
events.why: 76 galleries opening simultaneously with public programming at the New Museum — a rare moment when the city's gallery infrastructure becomes legible as a system, not just a series of separate rooms; worth moving through it intentionally rather than treating it as an art fair.

events.name: Doris Salcedo — New Exhibition Opening
events.why: Salcedo works with human hair, furniture, concrete — materials that carry body memory — to build structures about disappearance and political violence; two new bodies of work makes this the rare gallery opening worth treating as a destination.
